facts.fact: A basic twelve-bar blues uses three chords, built on the first, fourth and fifth notes of the scale and written as the I, IV and V chords.
facts.hook: a kid at a jam session asks what 'one-four-five' means before the band starts

facts.fact: In the most basic twelve-bar blues, the band stays on the I chord for the first four bars and moves to the IV chord in bar five.
facts.hook: a soloist changes notes a bar too early and clashes with the band

facts.fact: A blues in the key of A is usually played with the chords A7, D7 and E7, which are dominant seventh chords.
facts.hook: a guitarist and a pianist agree on the key and have to work out the three chords

facts.fact: The minor pentatonic scale has five notes; in A, they are A, C, D, E and G, and many blues solos are built from it.
facts.hook: a nervous player is told any of five notes will fit and starts to relax

facts.fact: The blues scale is the minor pentatonic scale with one extra note, the flattened fifth, which gives the music its gritty 'blue' sound.
facts.hook: one strange note suddenly makes a practice solo sound like real blues

facts.fact: One complete time through the twelve bars is called a chorus, and a soloist often plays several choruses in a row.
facts.hook: the band leader says 'take two choruses' and the soloist has to count

facts.fact: The turnaround is the end of the twelve-bar form, usually landing on the V chord, which pulls the music back to the start of the next chorus.
facts.hook: a soloist gets lost and finds the way back by listening for the turnaround

facts.fact: In jazz and blues jams, players often 'trade fours', taking turns to improvise four bars each.
facts.hook: two friends trade fours and try to answer each other's ideas

facts.fact: Bending a guitar string pushes it sideways and stretches it tighter, which raises the note's pitch.
facts.hook: a guitarist's bend goes too far and sounds sour

facts.fact: Many blues songs use a shuffle rhythm, in which each pair of eighth notes is played long-short instead of evenly.
facts.hook: a pianist plays the right notes but it sounds stiff until they learn the shuffle

facts.fact: Call and response, where one musical phrase is answered by another, is a key part of the blues and comes from African American work songs and church music.
facts.hook: a solo sounds better once the player answers their own phrase

facts.fact: The blues developed among African Americans in the Deep South of the United States in the second half of the 1800s.
facts.hook: a grandparent's old record starts a question about where the blues came from

facts.fact: Choral music is often written for four voice parts, soprano, alto, tenor and bass, from highest to lowest.
facts.hook: a new choir member has to choose which part to stand with

facts.fact: In a two-part choir of higher voices, the upper part is usually called soprano and the lower part alto.
facts.hook: a singer who thinks alto means 'less important' learns it just means lower

facts.fact: Two notes a third apart, such as C and E, sound smooth together, which is why a harmony line often runs a third below the melody.
facts.hook: the alto part finally clicks when a singer hears it sit just under the tune

facts.fact: Singing in unison means everyone sings the same notes; singing in harmony means different parts sing different notes at the same time.
facts.hook: a choir sounds thin until the second part comes in

facts.fact: In a round such as 'Row, Row, Row Your Boat', every group sings the same melody but starts at a different time, which creates harmony.
facts.hook: a choir warms up with a round and one group keeps jumping into the other's line

facts.fact: In staggered breathing, choir members take breaths at different moments, so a long note keeps sounding even though every singer breathes.
facts.hook: a choir learns to hold a note longer than any one singer could

facts.fact: During puberty the larynx grows, and a boy's singing voice typically drops by about an octave, which can move him to a different choir part.
facts.hook: a singer's voice cracks in rehearsal and the director suggests a new part

facts.fact: A conductor shows the first beat of each bar, called the downbeat, with a downward movement of the hand or baton.
facts.hook: a singer loses count and finds the place again by watching the conductor

facts.fact: Most modern tuning sets the A above middle C at 440 vibrations per second, or 440 hertz.
facts.hook: a pianist plays an A so the choir can find its starting note

facts.fact: A note one octave higher than another vibrates exactly twice as fast, which is why the two sound like the same note at different heights.
facts.hook: two singers think they are singing different notes but are an octave apart

facts.fact: When two singers hold nearly but not exactly the same pitch, the sound pulses with a wobble called beats, which slows and disappears as they match.
facts.hook: two altos listen for the wobble to fix a note that is slightly out of tune

facts.fact: The voice comes from two vocal folds in the larynx that vibrate as air passes between them; tightening them raises the pitch.
facts.hook: a singer strains for a high note and learns what is happening in their throat

facts.fact: Musical loudness is marked with Italian words: piano means soft and forte means loud.
facts.hook: a player sees 'p' on the page and plays it loudly anyway

facts.fact: Pianissimo, written pp, means very soft, and fortissimo, written ff, means very loud.
facts.hook: the band blasts through the ending that was marked pp

facts.fact: A crescendo means gradually getting louder, and a diminuendo or decrescendo means gradually getting softer.
facts.hook: the band gets loud all at once instead of building up

facts.fact: Tempo is measured in beats per minute, so a marking of 60 means one beat each second.
facts.hook: a drummer uses a clock's second hand to check a slow tempo

facts.fact: Johann Nepomuk Maelzel patented the mechanical metronome, a ticking device that sets a steady tempo, in 1815.
facts.hook: a player who rushes every piece tries a metronome for the first time

facts.fact: The piano's full name is pianoforte, meaning soft-loud, because the player can make notes soft or loud by how hard the keys are struck.
facts.hook: a pianist learns why a harder touch changes more than just the speed

facts.fact: Bartolomeo Cristofori, who looked after instruments for the Medici court in Florence, built the first successful piano around 1700.
facts.hook: a museum plaque starts a question about who invented the piano

facts.fact: Ritardando, often written rit., means gradually slowing down, and accelerando means gradually speeding up.
facts.hook: half the band slows at the rit. and the other half does not

facts.fact: The marking 'a tempo' tells players to return to the original speed after the music has slowed down or sped up.
facts.hook: a pianist keeps playing slowly after the rit. and misses the 'a tempo'

facts.fact: A fermata is a symbol over a note telling players to hold it longer than written, with the conductor deciding when to stop.
facts.hook: one trumpet cuts off early on the fermata

facts.fact: Italian tempo words describe speed: largo means very slow, andante means at a walking pace, and allegro means fast and lively.
facts.hook: a player guesses 'andante' means fast and the piece falls apart

facts.fact: On most pianos, the right-hand pedal lifts the dampers off the strings, so notes keep ringing after the keys are released.
facts.hook: a pianist holds the pedal down too long and the notes blur together

facts.fact: Sound is a vibration passed from particle to particle; each particle only moves back and forth, and the particles do not travel along with the sound.
facts.hook: a science-fair demo with a line of dominoes and a slinky

facts.fact: Sound cannot travel through empty space, because there are no particles there to pass the vibration along.
facts.hook: an argument over whether space battles in movies should be silent

facts.fact: In air, a sound wave is a series of compressions, where particles are squeezed together, and rarefactions, where they are spread apart.
facts.hook: a stretched slinky shows the bunched and spread parts of a wave

facts.fact: Sound moves faster in water than in air mainly because water is much harder to compress, so each molecule pushes on the next almost at once.
facts.hook: kids at a pool try to explain why they hear a tap underwater so clearly

facts.fact: Water is about 800 times denser than air, which on its own would slow sound down, but water's much greater stiffness more than makes up for it.
facts.hook: a student's science-fair poster says 'denser means faster' and a judge asks a question

facts.fact: Sound travels faster in warm air than in cold air, gaining about 0.6 meters per second for each degree Celsius.
facts.hook: two friends time an echo on a hot day and a cold day and get different answers

facts.fact: A sound's pitch depends on its frequency, the number of vibrations per second, measured in hertz; faster vibrations make a higher pitch.
facts.hook: a kid shortens a vibrating ruler over a table edge and hears the note rise

facts.fact: A sound's loudness depends on its amplitude, how far the particles move back and forth; bigger vibrations make louder sounds.
facts.hook: a drum hit harder makes the rice on top jump higher

facts.fact: Young people can usually hear frequencies from about 20 hertz up to about 20,000 hertz, and the top of that range drops with age.
facts.hook: a teen hears a high whine that their grandparent cannot

facts.fact: Sound makes the eardrum vibrate, and three tiny bones in the middle ear, the hammer, anvil and stirrup, pass the vibration to the inner ear.
facts.hook: a museum's giant ear model shows where a sound goes after it enters

facts.fact: Ships measure water depth with sonar: they send a pulse of sound down and time how long its echo takes to return from the seabed.
facts.hook: a science-museum exhibit lets visitors find the depth of a model lake

facts.fact: A struck tuning fork dipped in water flicks out spray, showing that its prongs are vibrating even though they move too fast to see.
facts.hook: a tuning fork seems perfectly still until someone touches it to water

facts.fact: Ohm's law says voltage equals current times resistance, so a wire's resistance is found by dividing the voltage across it by the current through it.
facts.hook: a science-fair team has two meter readings and needs the third number

facts.fact: If a wire has 6 volts across it and 2 amps flowing through it, its resistance is 6 divided by 2, which is 3 ohms.
facts.hook: a student multiplies instead of divides and gets a strange answer

facts.fact: Ohm's law is named after the German physicist Georg Simon Ohm, who published it in 1827.
facts.hook: a kid wonders why a unit of electricity has a person's name

facts.fact: Resistance is measured in ohms, written with the Greek letter omega.
facts.hook: a student mistakes the omega symbol on a meter for a horseshoe

facts.fact: An ammeter measures current and must be connected in series, in the same loop as the wire, so the current flows through the meter.
facts.hook: a meter reads zero because it was clipped on in the wrong place

facts.fact: A voltmeter measures voltage and is connected in parallel, with its two leads touching either end of the component being tested.
facts.hook: two lab partners argue about where the voltmeter leads should go

facts.fact: For wires of the same material and thickness, doubling the length doubles the resistance.
facts.hook: a team tests short and long pieces of the same wire and sees a pattern

facts.fact: A thicker wire of the same material and length has less resistance than a thinner one, because current has more room to flow.
facts.hook: a thin wire gives a surprising reading compared with a thick one

facts.fact: A metal wire's resistance rises as it heats up, so Ohm's law gives a steady resistance only while the wire's temperature stays the same.
facts.hook: readings drift as a wire warms up during a long test

facts.fact: For a metal wire at constant temperature, a graph of voltage against current is a straight line through zero, and its slope is the resistance.
facts.hook: a science-fair graph turns five readings into one clear answer

facts.fact: Current measured in milliamps must be changed into amps before using Ohm's law; 250 milliamps is 0.25 amps.
facts.hook: a resistance answer comes out a thousand times too small

facts.fact: The volt, the unit of voltage, is named after the Italian physicist Alessandro Volta.
facts.hook: a kid spots Volta's name on a museum exhibit about batteries

facts.fact: Closing a switch completes the circuit so current flows; opening it makes a gap, and the current stops everywhere in the loop at once.
facts.hook: a model house's lights will not switch on until a loose wire is found

facts.fact: An ordinary incandescent bulb lights because current heats its thin filament, typically above 2,000 degrees Celsius, until it glows white-hot.
facts.hook: a kid wonders why an old bulb is too hot to touch after it has been on

facts.fact: Bulb filaments are made of tungsten because it has the highest melting point of any pure metal, about 3,400 degrees Celsius.
facts.hook: a science-museum display shows a filament under a magnifier

facts.fact: An incandescent bulb is filled with an unreactive gas such as argon, because the hot filament would quickly burn out if it met oxygen.
facts.hook: a cracked bulb flashes once and dies

facts.fact: A battery turns stored chemical energy into electrical energy, and it goes flat when those chemicals are used up.
facts.hook: a circuit that worked yesterday stays dark today

facts.fact: A standard AA battery provides about 1.5 volts.
facts.hook: two kids work out how many batteries their project needs

facts.fact: Circuit diagrams show current flowing from positive to negative, but the electrons in the wires actually move from negative to positive.
facts.hook: a student is puzzled when a book says the arrows point the 'wrong' way

facts.fact: Metals such as copper conduct electricity well, while plastic and rubber are insulators, which is why wires are copper covered in plastic.
facts.hook: a kid strips a wire and sees the shiny metal inside the plastic

facts.fact: When two identical bulbs are wired in series to one battery, each glows more dimly than a single bulb would on the same battery.
facts.hook: adding a second bulb makes the model lighthouse dimmer, not brighter

facts.fact: In a series circuit, if one bulb breaks, the loop is broken and every bulb in it goes out.
facts.hook: one dead bulb makes a whole string of lights go dark

facts.fact: In a parallel circuit, each bulb has its own path to the battery, so the others stay lit if one bulb breaks.
facts.hook: a team rewires their project so one broken bulb cannot ruin it

facts.fact: A short circuit, a wire joining a battery's two ends with nothing in between, lets a large current flow that can make the wire and battery dangerously hot.
facts.hook: a teacher stops a kid from joining the battery ends with bare wire and explains why

facts.fact: Average speed equals distance travelled divided by the time taken.
facts.hook: two friends race marbles and need a fair way to compare them

facts.fact: A ball that rolls 3 meters in 2 seconds has an average speed of 1.5 meters per second.
facts.hook: a hallway race is measured with a tape measure and a stopwatch

facts.fact: On a distance-time graph, time goes along the horizontal axis and distance goes up the vertical axis.
facts.hook: a student swaps the axes and the graph makes no sense

facts.fact: On a distance-time graph, a straight sloping line means the object is moving at a constant speed.
facts.hook: a ball on a smooth floor makes a surprisingly straight line on the graph

facts.fact: On a distance-time graph, a steeper line means a faster speed.
facts.hook: two balls' lines on one graph settle who won the race

facts.fact: On a distance-time graph, a flat horizontal line means the object is not moving.
facts.hook: a flat stretch on the graph shows where the ball got stuck

facts.fact: On a distance-time graph, a line that curves upward and gets steeper shows an object speeding up.
facts.hook: a ball rolling down a skate-park ramp makes a curved line

facts.fact: A person's reaction time on a stopwatch is often about a fifth of a second, so timing a longer run makes that error matter less.
facts.hook: two timers get different results for the same roll

facts.fact: Repeating a measurement several times and taking the average gives a more reliable result than a single try.
facts.hook: one odd reading nearly ruins a science-fair result

facts.fact: Galileo studied motion by rolling balls down gentle ramps, which slowed the motion enough for him to time it.
facts.hook: a science-museum ramp exhibit copies Galileo's idea

facts.fact: To change a speed in meters per second into kilometers per hour, multiply it by 3.6.
facts.hook: a kid wants to know if their ball beat a walking person

facts.fact: A ball rolling on a flat floor gradually slows down because friction and rolling resistance take away its energy.
facts.hook: a ball rolls far on smooth tile but stops quickly on carpet

facts.fact: Washing your hands before touching a cut helps keep germs from getting into the wound.
facts.hook: a kid about to help a younger cousin with a scraped knee stops to wash first

facts.fact: Most small cuts stop bleeding when firm, steady pressure is pressed on them with a clean cloth or bandage for about 10 minutes.
facts.hook: a paper-cut-turned-kitchen-cut keeps bleeding because someone keeps peeking

facts.fact: Raising a bleeding hand or arm above the level of the heart helps reduce blood flow to the wound.
facts.hook: a grandparent tells a kid to hold their cut hand up high

facts.fact: A cut should be rinsed under clean running water to wash out dirt before it is covered.
facts.hook: a scraped elbow at the skate park gets rinsed at a water fountain

facts.fact: Mayo Clinic advises against cleaning a cut with hydrogen peroxide or iodine, because both can irritate the wound.
facts.hook: a kid reaches for the fizzing bottle and a first-aid guide says otherwise

facts.fact: A thin layer of petroleum jelly or antibiotic ointment keeps a cut's surface moist, which helps it heal and can reduce scarring.
facts.hook: two friends argue whether a cut should be left to dry out

facts.fact: A bandage should be changed at least once a day, or any time it gets wet or dirty.
facts.hook: a soggy bandage after swimming needs replacing

facts.fact: A cut that is still bleeding after 10 minutes of firm pressure needs medical help, and the pressure should continue until help arrives.
facts.hook: a kid keeps pressing on a cut while an adult calls for help

facts.fact: A cut whose edges gape open may need stitches, skin glue or closure strips from a doctor or nurse to heal well.
facts.hook: a deep cut from a broken glass will not stay closed under a bandage

facts.fact: Spreading redness, swelling, warmth, pus or worsening pain around a cut can be signs of infection and a reason to see a doctor.
facts.hook: a cut that looked fine two days ago is now red and hot

facts.fact: A doctor may give a tetanus shot after a deep or dirty wound, because tetanus bacteria live in soil and dust.
facts.hook: a kid cuts their hand on a rusty garden tool at a grandparent's house

facts.fact: An animal bite that breaks the skin should be checked by a doctor, because bites can carry germs deep into the wound.
facts.hook: a friend's dog nips a kid's hand and the adults decide what to do

facts.fact: Most bicycle tyres have a separate inner tube inside that holds the air, so a flat usually means a hole in the tube.
facts.hook: a kid expects to replace the whole tyre and learns only the tube is broken

facts.fact: Bike tubes use two common valve types: the thin Presta valve and the wider Schrader valve, the same kind used on car tyres.
facts.hook: a pump will not fit the valve and a kid learns there are two kinds

facts.fact: A Presta valve has a small nut on top that must be unscrewed before any air can be pumped in or let out.
facts.hook: a kid pumps hard and nothing happens

facts.fact: Letting all the air out of the tube first makes the tyre loose enough to lever off the rim.
facts.hook: a tyre lever will not budge until the last air is let out

facts.fact: To remove a tyre, a tyre lever is hooked under the tyre's edge and clipped to a spoke, then a second lever is used a little further along.
facts.hook: two levers do what bare fingers could not

facts.fact: A tyre's recommended pressure is printed on its sidewall, often in psi or bar.
facts.hook: a kid guesses the pressure and the tyre feels soft

facts.fact: A slow leak can be found by pumping some air into the tube and holding it under water to watch for bubbles.
facts.hook: a tube in a bucket of water at a grandparent's house reveals a tiny hole

facts.fact: Before fitting a new tube, the inside of the tyre should be checked for the thorn or glass that caused the flat, or it will puncture again.
facts.hook: a new tube goes flat on the first ride

facts.fact: Putting a little air in a new tube before fitting it gives it shape, so it is less likely to twist or get pinched under the tyre.
facts.hook: a floppy tube keeps getting caught as the tyre goes back on

facts.fact: A pinch flat, often called a snakebite, is two small parallel slits made when an under-inflated tyre hits a sharp edge like a kerb.
facts.hook: a kid finds two neat holes side by side after hitting a kerb

facts.fact: When patching a tube with glue-on patches, the glue must be left to dry until it is no longer wet before the patch is pressed on.
facts.hook: an impatient patch job peels off within a mile

facts.fact: In 1888, John Boyd Dunlop, a Scottish vet living in Belfast, patented an air-filled tyre he had first made for his son's tricycle.
facts.hook: a kid fixing a flat wonders who invented tyres full of air

facts.fact: Counting up is a quick way to check change: start at the price and add each coin and note handed back until you reach the amount you paid.
facts.hook: a kid at the corner store is unsure the change is right and counts up

facts.fact: If milk costs 2.65 and you pay with 5.00, the correct change is 2.35, whatever the currency.
facts.hook: a cashier hands back too little and the kid notices

facts.fact: In the United States and Canada, shelf prices usually leave out sales tax, which is added at the till; in the UK and EU, shown prices already include VAT.
facts.hook: a kid brings the exact shelf price and is still a few cents short

facts.fact: Since Canada stopped distributing pennies in 2013, cash totals there are rounded to the nearest five cents, while card payments are still charged to the exact cent.
facts.hook: a total of 3.02 becomes 3.00 when a kid pays in cash

facts.fact: Many stores stock shelves 'first in, first out', putting older products at the front, so the carton with the latest date is often at the back.
facts.hook: a kid checks the dates and reaches behind the front row of milk

facts.fact: Many shelf labels show a unit price, such as the price per litre, so different sizes can be compared; the bigger carton is often, but not always, cheaper per litre.
facts.hook: a kid has to decide between one big carton and two small ones

facts.fact: In countries where cars drive on the left, such as the United Kingdom, Japan and Australia, the nearest lane of traffic comes from your right.
facts.hook: a visiting cousin looks the wrong way before crossing

facts.fact: A receipt lists every item and the amount paid, so reading it before leaving the till catches a scanning mistake while it is easy to fix.
facts.hook: milk scanned twice is noticed on the receipt

facts.fact: US food safety guidance says perishable food such as milk should not sit out for more than two hours, or one hour above 32 degrees Celsius.
facts.hook: a kid stops at a friend's house on a hot day with the milk in the bag

facts.fact: US food safety agencies advise keeping a refrigerator at 4 degrees Celsius, or 40 degrees Fahrenheit, or colder.
facts.hook: milk goes sour early and a kid checks the fridge dial

facts.fact: Most pasteurized milk has been heated to at least 72 degrees Celsius for 15 seconds and then cooled quickly, which kills harmful bacteria.
facts.hook: a kid reads 'pasteurized' on the carton and asks what it means

facts.fact: Homogenized milk has had its fat broken into tiny droplets that stay mixed, so a layer of cream does not rise to the top.
facts.hook: milk from a farm shop has cream on top and store milk does not
